work: Adversus Praxean (cited via Newman, Arians of the Fourth Century, ch. 2 sec. 3)
ref: Adv. Prax. 19.7-8 (Latin Library division; Newman gives no chapter number; identified by matching wording)
latin: ostendimus etiam duos deos in scriptura relatos et duos dominos: [8] et tamen ne de isto scandalizentur, rationem reddimus qua dei non duo dicantur nec domini sed qua pater et filius duo, et hoc non ex separatione substantiae sed ex dispositione, cum individuum et inseparatum filium a patre pronuntiamus
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked
english: We declare that two are revealed as God in Scripture, two as Lord; but we explain ourselves, lest offence should be taken. They are not called two, in respect of their both being God, or Lord, but in respect of their being Father and Son; and this moreover, not from any division of substance, but from mutual relation, since we pronounce the Son to be individual with and inseparable from the Father.
translator: John Henry Newman (his own rendering, in Arians)
page: 167 (Newman 3rd ed., marker {167} precedes the passage; {168} follows)
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: Newman quotes Tertullian that the plural "two Gods/Lords" are Father and Son by relation, not by division of substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (distinction without division of substance)
limits: Newman quotes it as an apologetic point, not as a full exegesis of the 19.7-8 argument; Latin Library edition unnamed; Latin is copied from that page, not from Kroymann.

work: Adversus Praxean (cited via Newman, Arians, ch. 2 sec. 3, note 42)
ref: Adv. Prax. 3.1 (Latin Library division; Newman's note 42 gives no chapter, identified by content)
latin: Simplices enim quique, ne dixerim imprudentes et idiotae, quae maior semper credentium pars est, quoniam et ipsa regula fidei a pluribus diis saeculi ad unicum et verum deum transfert, non intellegentes unicum quidem sed cum sua oeconomia esse credendum, expavescunt ad oeconomiam. numerum et dispositionem trinitatis divisionem praesumunt unitatis, quando unitas ex semetipsa derivans trinitatem non destruatur ab illa sed administretur.
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked
english: Thus Tertullian says, that it is a mistake "to suppose that the number and arrangement of the Trinity is a division of its Unity; inasmuch as the Unity drawing out the Trinity from itself, is not destroyed by it, but is subserved."
translator: John Henry Newman (his own rendering, in Arians)
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: Newman quotes Tertullian denying that the number and arrangement of the Trinity divides the Unity.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (unity and Trinity held together in the economy)
limits: Newman's English is a loose rendering; "Trinity" stands for Tertullian's trinitas; the same Latin is the basis of the objection that Tertullian says "economy" (oeconomia) rather than "substance".

latin: ita connexus patris in filio et filii in paracleto tres efficit cohaerentes alterum ex altero. qui tres unum sunt, non unus, quomodo dictum est, Ego et pater unum sumus, ad substantiae unitatem non ad numeri singularitatem.
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked | Newman (p.178) prints a different Latin: "Connexus Patris in Filio, et Filii in Paracleto, tres efficit coh?rentes, qui tres unum sint, non unus." (the newmanreader HTML garbles "cohaerentes" into a mojibake sequence, shown as ?; sint vs sunt; alterum ex altero omitted)
english: Thus the connection of the Father in the Son, and of the Son in the Paraclete, produces three coherent Persons, who are yet distinct One from Another. These Three are one essence, not one Person, as it is said, I and my Father are One, John 10:30 in respect of unity of substance not singularity of number.
page: pp. 597-632 (Against Praxeas in ANF vol. 3; exact page not captured)
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe, 1885; Christian Literature Co.); Against Praxeas per fourthcentury.com listing pp. 597-632 (search result, listing not opened); exact page not captured
what_it_says: Tertullian calls the Father, Son and Paraclete three coherent Persons of one essence, not one Person, citing John 10:30 for unity of substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (unity of substance with distinction of Persons)
limits: Newman and the Latin Library differ in the Latin (sint/sunt, alterum ex altero); which reading the Kroymann edition has is not checked. Tertullian says "tres ... coherentes" and not "consubstantial"; the word "essence" is the translator's choice.

latin: Omnia, inquit, patris mea sunt: cur non et nomina? cum ergo legis Deum omnipotentem et Altissimum et Deum virtutum et Regem Israelis et Qui est, vide ne per haec filius etiam demonstretur suo iure Deus <omnipotens> qua sermo Dei omnipotentis
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked
english: Tertullian, after quoting the text, "All that the Father hath are Mine," adds, "If so, why should not the Father's titles be His? When then we read that God is Almighty, and the Highest, and the God of Hosts, and the King of Israel, and Jehovah, see to it whether the Son also be not signified by these passages, as being in His own right the Almighty God, inasmuch as He is the Word of the Almighty God." | ANF (Holmes) for the same passage: "All things, says He, which the Father has are mine. John 16:15 Then why not His names also?"
translator: John Henry Newman (his own rendering, in Arians); ANF part by Peter Holmes
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: Tertullian argues that the Son shares the Father's titles (Almighty, Most High, God of hosts) because the Son is the Word of God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (divinity of the Son through shared titles)
limits: Newman's English is not the Latin; the Latin given is from the Latin Library; the Son's title argument is a divinity claim, not a statement of co-equality.

work: Adversus Praxean (cited via Newman, Arians, ch. 2 sec. 4, note 20 "Tertull. in Prax. 7, 8, abridged")
ref: Adv. Prax. 7.5 (Latin Library division); Newman says "7, 8, abridged"
latin: ergo, inquis, das aliquam substantiam esse sermonem, spiritu et sophia et ratione constructam? plane. non vis enim eum substantivum habere in re per substantiae proprietatem, ut res et persona quaedam videri� possit et ita capiat secundus a deo constitutus duos efficere,� patrem et filium, deum et sermonem
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked | Latin Library text contains a stray replacement character (rendered here as �) after "videri" and "efficere," that is an encoding artifact of that page; check Kroymann.
english: "Can the Word of God," he asks, "be unsubstantial, who is called the Son, who is even named God? ... Whatever then has been the substance of the Word, that, I call a Person, and claim for it the name of Son, and being such, He comes next to the Father."
translator: John Henry Newman (his own rendering, in Arians; abridged)
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: Newman reports Tertullian insisting that the Word has a substance and is a Person, while using probole only in a non-Valentinian sense.
use: answer to objection (the Son as "second" and as having substance)
limits: Newman abridges and paraphrases; the ellipsis is his. Newman adds that Tertullian was "obliged to apologize" for the word, which is Newman's judgment, not Tertullian's.

work: Adversus Hermogenem (cited via Newman, Arians, Appendix Note 2, "The Doctrine of the Divine Gennesis")
latin: Fuit autem tempus cum ei delictum et filius non fuit quod iudicem et qui patrem dominum faceret.
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked (Adv. Herm.: Latin Library page, same caveats)
english: Newman writes: "There was a time when the Son was not," says Tertullian (adv. Herm. 3). ANF (Holmes) for Adv. Herm. 3: "There was, however, a time when neither sin existed with Him, nor the Son; the former of which was to constitute the Lord a Judge, and the latter a Father."
translator: Newman (his paraphrase, not verbatim); ANF Adv. Herm. translated by Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, per newadvent page)
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: The Latin says there was a time when there was no sin and no Son, so that God was not yet Judge or Father; Newman's English "the Son was not" is a shortening.
limits: The sentence is about the titles Judge and Father (conditions for those titles), not directly about the Son's eternal being; Newman's "the Son was not" is not verbatim.

work: Arians of the Fourth Century, Appendix Note 2 (Newman, on Bull)
ref: Newman, Appendix Note 2, pp. 417-418 (the passage refers to Bull's treatment of ante-Nicene "generation" language, including Tertullian)
english: his defence of them is but a confirmation of a foregone conclusion; he starts with the assumption that the words of the early writers cannot mean what they naturally do mean; and, though this bias is worthy of all respect, still the fact that it exists is a call on us to examine closely arguments which without it would not have been used.
edition: John Henry Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 3rd ed. (London: Longmans, Green, 1871); newmanreader.org text carries the 3rd-ed. page markers {n}
what_it_says: Newman says Bull's accommodation of ante-Nicene generation language starts from a conclusion that the words cannot mean what they say.
use: objection (Newman's judgment against the accommodation reading that Bull uses)
limits: Newman's critique is general (Bull, Maran, the Ballerini) and not specific to Tertullian. It is Newman's judgment, and Newman also says the bias is "worthy of all respect".

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII "The doctrine of Tertullian concerning the consubstantiality of the Son..."
english: Read only his single work against Praxeas, in which he treats fully and professedly of the most holy Trinity; he there asserts the consubstantiality of the Son so frequently and so plainly, that you would suppose the author had written after the time of the Nicene council.
translator: not named in the volume (title page: "A New Translation"; translator not found in front matter)
page: 193 (running head on PDF page 215; chapter-title line reads "93" in the text layer)
edition: Bull, A Defence of the Nicene Creed, A New Translation (Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851), Library of Anglo-Catholic Theology; scan archive.org libraryofangbull01oxfouoft
what_it_says: Bull says Tertullian in the Adversus Praxean asserts the Son's consubstantiality so plainly that he might be writing after Nicaea.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (secondary defender, read at first hand)
limits: Bull is a partisan defender of Nicaea, writing in 1685; "consubstantiality" is Bull's term. Kaye (item below) reports Bull admitting some expressions at variance with co-eternity.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII sec. 2
ref: Bull cites Adv. Prax. ch. 4 (Latin Library division: 4.1)
latin: Filium non aliunde deduco, sed de SUBSTANTIA PATRIS. (Bull, footnote, p.195 [p. 502 of Bull's Latin]); Latin Library Adv. Prax. 4.1: "...qui filium non aliunde deduco, sed de substantia patris, nihil facientem sine patris voluntate..."
latin_edition: Bull's Latin footnote (Burton/Grabe edition, not named precisely); Latin Library text: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked
english: Tertullian: "I derive not the Son from any other source, but from THE SUBSTANCE OF THE Father." (OCR of the scan reads "Fatuer"; the word is Father.) | ANF (Holmes), Adv. Prax. 4: "...who derive the Son from no other source but from the substance of the Father..."
translator: not named (Bull LACT translation); ANF by Peter Holmes
edition: Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed (Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull quotes Tertullian that the Son is derived from no other source than the Father's substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son and Father of one substance)
limits: "Derive" (deduco) is the term that Arians and Sabellians read in opposite ways; Bull reads it as consubstantial. Latin is from two sources, not one edition.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII sec. 2
ref: Bull cites Adv. Prax. ch. 12 (Latin Library: 12.7)
latin: Caeterum ubique teneo unam substantiam in tribus coherentibus. (Bull footnote, p.195 [p. 506 of Bull's Latin]); Latin Library 12.7: "ceterum <etsi> ubique teneo unam substantiam in tribus cohaerentibus..."
latin_edition: Bull footnote (Latin); Latin Library: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked (the <etsi> is the page's own insertion, absent from Bull)
english: "Still," he says, "I every where hold one substance in three coherent [Persons]." | ANF (Holmes), Adv. Prax. 12: "But although I must everywhere hold one only substance in three coherent and inseparable (Persons)..."
translator: not named (Bull LACT translation); ANF by Peter Holmes
edition: Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed (Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Tertullian says he holds one substance in three coherent Persons.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (one substance, three coherent)
limits: "coherentes" is read by Bull and Newman as "coherent [Persons]"; the Latin is a participle and the English "Persons" is supplied. Tertullian in the same chapter then says the Son is "another" (alium) in the economy.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII sec. 2
ref: Bull on Adv. Prax. 9 ("portio") and 14 (sun and ray)
english: A part is less than the whole from which it is taken; the Son, however, is in all respects, (excepting that He is the Son,) like, and equal to the Father, and has and possesses all that the Father has.
edition: Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed (Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull answers the "portion" language: a part is less than its whole, but the Son is equal to the Father in all but being Son.
use: answer to objection (portio totius; Father greater)
limits: Bull's answer is an assertion of equality by stipulation; it does not discuss John 14:28 ("Father is greater") in this sentence. Adv. Prax. 9.2 says the Son is "derivatio totius et portio" and that the Father is greater.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII sec. 2
ref: Bull on Adv. Prax. 14 (Latin Library: 14.3-4 area)
latin: sicut nec solem nobis contemplari licet quantum ad ipsam substantiae summam quae est in caelis, radium autem eius toleramus oculis pro temperatura portionis quae in terram inde porrigitur.
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked (Latin is Tertullian's sentence from Adv. Prax. 14, quoted by Bull at p.200)
english: When, however, Tertullian, in his treatise against Praxeas, chap. 14, compares together the Father and the Son by an analogy derived from the sun, ... and its ray, whose brightness is endurable, "tempered as it is by its being only a portion" ... it must be understood (unless you are disposed to charge Tertullian with the grossest contradiction) of that economy which the Son of God, out of His great love to the human race, voluntarily undertook; by which, that is to say, ever since the fall of the first man, He condescended, and made Himself, so far as might be, visible to holy men ...
edition: Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed (Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull reads Tertullian's sun-and-ray analogy as describing the Son's economic manifestation to humans, not a lesser nature.
use: answer to objection (invisible Father / visible Son, Adv. Prax. 14)
limits: Bull's reading is an accommodation; the Latin says "portio" of the sun's ray and "summa substantiae"; the English is assembled from two-column OCR (PDF 222-223); the OCR garbles "understood" ("underBerea stood") from a header overprint, so check the scan for the exact wording.

work: Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (George Bull), ch. VII sec. 8 (against Sandius)
ref: Bull, ch. VII sec. 8 (dating of Adv. Prax.; Bull quotes its opening, Adv. Prax. 1)
english: For Tertullian himself expressly professes, and that in this very treatise against Praxeas, that even at the time he was writing, he was already dissevered from "the carnal," as he called them, that is from the catholics, and had joined himself to the party of Montanus.
edition: Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed (Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull argues against Sandius that Tertullian wrote Adv. Prax. while already a Montanist, so a Montanist date cannot explain its orthodoxy.
use: context (dating and Montanist setting of Adv. Prax.)
limits: Bull's own argument; the dating and Montanist claim are contested; OCR was cleaned of hyphenation and stray characters.

latin: pater enim tota substantia est, filius vero, derivatio totius et portio, sicut ipse profitetur, Quia pater maior me est: a quo et minoratus canitur in psalmo, Modicum quid citra angelos.
latin_edition: Latin Library text (thelatinlibrary.com); no edition named on the page; CAPUT and [n] markers as printed there; Kroymann/Evans not checked
english: For the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as He Himself acknowledges: My Father is greater than I. John 14:28 In the Psalm His inferiority is described as being a little lower than the angels.
page: pp. 597-632 (ANF vol. 3; exact page not captured)
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe, 1885; Christian Literature Co.); Against Praxeas per fourthcentury.com listing pp. 597-632 (search result, listing not opened); exact page not captured
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Father is the whole substance and the Son a derivation and portion of it, and that the Father is greater.
use: objection (the Son is a part and the Father greater); answer is the Bull item above and Adv. Prax. 9.1 ("nec divisione alium sed distinctione")
limits: This is the hard passage itself; the Latin is from the Latin Library page, unnamed edition; the Holmes English is not checked against Kroymann.

work: Some Account of the Writings and Opinions of Tertullian (Bishop John Kaye, 1826), as appended in ANF vol. 3 (Holmes)
ref: Kaye pp. 504-596 (range cited in the ANF note); the Hermogenes passage is cited there as "Ch. iii. compared with ch. xviii."
english: As, therefore, there was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed, the titles of Judge and Father were not at that time applicable to God. (Kaye's own account of Adv. Herm. 3, in context: Hermogenes held matter eternal; Tertullian said God was not always Lord.)
translator: John Kaye (English original); reprinted in ANF vol. 3 by Holmes
page: Kaye pp. 504-596 (range; exact page not captured)
edition: ANF vol. 3 notes (Holmes/Coxe), reprinted text from Kaye 1826
what_it_says: Kaye explains the "time when the Son was not" passage as an argument against Hermogenes about the titles Lord, Judge and Father.
use: answer to objection (context of Adv. Herm. 3)
limits: Kaye (also quoted in Bull) concedes that for Wisdom and the Son Tertullian assigns "a beginning of existence" (next item). Kaye's account is 19th century and is an apology.

work: Some Account of the Writings and Opinions of Tertullian (Bishop John Kaye), as appended in ANF vol. 3
ref: Kaye, ANF vol. 3 note on Tertullian (Adv. Herm. ch. 3 compared with ch. 18)
english: Bp. Bull also, who conceives the language of Tertullian to be explicit and correct on the subject of the pre-existence and the consubstantiality, admits that he occasionally uses expressions at variance with the co-eternity of Christ. For instance, in the Tract against Hermogenes, ... we find a passage in which it is expressly asserted that there was a time when the Son was not.
translator: John Kaye (English original); reprinted in ANF vol. 3
page: Kaye pp. 504-596 (range; exact page not captured)
what_it_says: Kaye reports that Bull admits Tertullian sometimes writes at variance with the co-eternity of the Son, and gives Adv. Herm. 3 as the example.
use: objection (a Trinitarian apologist admits a hard passage)
limits: This is Kaye's report of Bull, not Bull's own words; the Bull text on the Hermogenes passage in the Defensio copy I read (archive.org vol. 1) was not found (see notes.md).

work: Some Account of the Writings and Opinions of Tertullian (Bishop John Kaye), as appended in ANF vol. 3
ref: Kaye, ANF vol. 3 note on Tertullian (on Hermogenes, and the Son's beginning)
english: But with respect to Wisdom and the Son (Sophia and Filius) the case is different. Tertullian assigns to both a beginning of existence: Sophia was created or formed in order to devise the plan of the universe; and the Son was begotten in order to carry that plan into effect.
translator: John Kaye (English original); reprinted in ANF vol. 3
page: Kaye pp. 504-596 (range; exact page not captured)
what_it_says: Kaye says Tertullian gives the Son a beginning of existence, although the Logos/Reason is not temporal.
use: objection (subordinationist concession from a sympathetic reader)
limits: Kaye adds that Bull describes the Reason and Spirit as co-eternal, and the titles Word and Son as applying only after creation; the Latin for that claim is not checked.

work: Some Account of the Writings and Opinions of Tertullian (Bishop John Kaye), as appended in ANF vol. 3
ref: Kaye, ANF vol. 3 note on Tertullian (general statement on Tertullian's language on the Trinity)
english: We are far from meaning to assert that expressions may not occasionally be found which are capable of a different interpretation, and which were carefully avoided by the orthodox writers of later times, when the controversies respecting the Trinity had introduced greater precision of language.
translator: John Kaye (English original); reprinted in ANF vol. 3
page: Kaye pp. 504-596 (range; exact page not captured)
what_it_says: Kaye concedes that Tertullian has expressions open to other readings, which later orthodox writers avoided.
use: objection (general concession that some expressions are hard); context for the method of reading
limits: This is Kaye's general concession; it is followed by Kaye's defence that the general tenor of Tertullian is Trinitarian (the Semler point, that picking expressions is not the way to read an author).
